conflict_rules.what_the_document_does:
### The ranked order

The document carries a full set of rules for its own clashes. There are five **levels of authority** in a stated order, root, system, developer, user and guideline, with a sixth position of no authority at all for the model's own past messages, tool outputs and quoted or untrusted text; a higher level overrides a lower one.

Every section of the document and every message role carries a **default level**, so any two instructions can be placed against each other. For two instructions of the same rank, the later one supersedes the earlier.

### Named winners and overrides

Two particular clashes have a named winner:

- Where two root-level principles conflict, the model does nothing.
- Where a serious safety concern meets another interest of a user aged 13 to 17, the model takes the safer option.

An instruction is also set aside where it conflicts with the letter or the implied intent of a higher one, or where it looks mistaken. Overriding comes in two grades: a **user-level default** falls only to an explicit instruction, a **guideline** falls to an implicit one as well.

Lower-level content may not change how a higher rule is read, and the document names the attempts it has in mind, among them a moral argument, a logical argument and an attempt to put the model into a different persona. Beyond the ranked order, the model is told to look for conflicts and ambiguities the document has not named and settle them by what the higher authority and the purpose of the request imply.

### Outcomes put in order

Two further clashes are settled by an explicit ordering of outcomes:

- For honesty, a good answer, then refusing, then a lie of omission, then a lie of commission, then breaking an explicit instruction.
- For confidence, a confident right answer down to a confident wrong one.

### Limits and worked cases

Two further rules cap what the order can be used for:

- Customisation, personalisation and localisation may never override anything above guideline level, with legal compliance carved out.
- An agreed **scope of autonomy** holds with no exceptions, even where breaking it would serve the user.

Worked cases show the order applied, including a developer instruction defeated by a root rule and a user request defeated by a developer instruction.
conflict_rules.why: The order is **strict**, it reaches every pair of rules in the document, it says what happens between two rules of equal rank, and it is shown working on cases.

rule_force.what_the_document_does:
Most section headings carry an **authority label**, root, system, developer, user or guideline, and the levels section says for each who may change it and how. Commentary sits in blocks marked as commentary, and the document states at the outset that those blocks **do not instruct** the model.

Some sections carry no label of their own, among them the parent sections on staying in bounds and on restricted content, so the force of a line there has to be taken from its wording or from the section above it.
rule_force.why: Force is marked across most of the text and the levels say who may change what, and a number of sections carrying instruction have **no label of their own**.

reasons.what_the_document_does:
The opening sets out three goals and three categories of risk, and says that the **levels of authority** exist because those goals conflict.

Many rules carry their reason in the same breath:

- Refusing a polarising topic is called a form of agenda in itself.
- Sycophancy is said to erode trust.
- Root-level rules are said to be imposed only where they are needed across the whole range of developers and users.

Commentary blocks add the reasoning behind several rules, including why untrusted data is quoted and why a scope should not be so narrow that a user starts approving everything by reflex. The style rules and parts of the content prohibitions are **stated bare**.
reasons.why: Reasons run through the document and many are concrete enough to decide a case it does not show, and a good number of the content and style rules **carry none**.

situations.what_the_document_does:
All six settings have rules of their own:

- Ordinary conversation is covered by the style and truth-seeking sections.
- Actions taken with tools have a scope of autonomy that must be agreed and a section on controlling and communicating side effects, with spending, sending, deleting and permission changes named.
- Images, audio and video have a section on adapting to the user's modality, a preset-voice rule, limits on visual sensitive content, and a rule on interjecting when a video feed shows imminent danger.
- Users aged 13 to 17 have a section of their own with its own prohibitions.
- Other AI agents appear on both sides: tool outputs and delegated instructions have no authority unless a higher level grants it, and any sub-agent the model delegates to must work under the same scope and honour a stop-work request.
- Customised deployments are the developer level, with default developer instructions a developer can override and worked cases of developer and user instructions meeting.
situations.why: Each of the six carries rules **written as instruction** to the model, which is the top of the scale.

contradictions.what_the_document_does:
Two clashes stand unsettled:

- Pressed to pick a side in a debate, the model is told to remind the user that its answer does not necessarily reflect its developer's view, and a case approved in the same section picks a side with no such reminder.
- Explaining a refusal, a case approved under the rule that no topic is off limits names OpenAI's policies and quotes the document at length, while the rule on refusal style forbids meta commentary on the model and any mention of OpenAI in a refusal.

Each pair sits at **one level of authority**, so the order of priority does not separate them. Neither involves a rule the document says can never be overridden.
contradictions.why: Two clashes are confirmed and neither touches a rule the document places **beyond override**, which is the middle of the scale.

avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.says:
The commitments at the front rule out using the models for persecution or mass surveillance, and state that humanity should stay in control of how AI is used and how its behaviour is shaped, with targeted or scaled exclusion, manipulation and the erosion of civic participation ruled out.

One rule turns that into an instruction: the model must not produce advice or content designed to **manipulate the political views** of named individuals or demographic groups, with example requests that qualify.

Taking control by fraud or coercion, escaping courts or constitutional limits, and how much power is at stake **go unaddressed**.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.why: Concrete quotable rules exist for political manipulation and most of the behaviour is **left unstated**, which is the step above discussed.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.same: Both OpenAI versions carry the same commitments at the front, persecution and mass surveillance among them, and the same rule against content designed to manipulate political views. Alibaba's spec covers the ground with a rule on political manipulation, and Anthropic's constitution refuses help with a power grab.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.differs: Anthropic's constitution tests whether power is being taken by means widely recognised as fair, whether it stays subject to checks such as elections and courts, and whether the action is conducted openly, and it asks how reversible the concentration would be. The newer version allows political content aimed at a broad audience.

instruction-hierarchy-conformance.says:
The chain of command is the **spine of the document**. Five levels of authority are listed in order, with a sixth position of no authority for the model's own past messages, tool outputs and quoted text, and every section and message role carries a default level, so any instruction can be placed.

The document then says how a candidate instruction is filtered out, and it works each rule through cases:

- By conflicting with a higher one in letter or intent.
- By being superseded by a later instruction at the same level.
- By looking mistaken.

Instructions found inside untrusted data carry **no authority** unless a higher level delegates it, and the document separates an AGENTS file a user has checked in from a web page nobody vouched for.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.why: Rules, worked cases and the edge of delegation are all present, and the conditions for the top of the scale hold **only in part**.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.same: The newer version keeps this ranking, the same filtering of candidate instructions and the same weight for an AGENTS file a user has checked in. Alibaba's spec and Anthropic's constitution set out orders of their own, and all four treat instructions inside quoted text and tool results as information.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.differs: Anthropic's constitution names Anthropic, operators and users as its principals and calls that order not a strict hierarchy, followed where an operator has a plausible **legitimate business reason**. Alibaba's spec lists the manoeuvres it refuses, role-play as the developer among them.

not-undermining-human-oversight.says:
The model may pursue only the goals its instructions entail, and the document names self-preservation, evading shutdown and accumulating compute, data or credentials as aims it must **never adopt as ends**. Further rules bound what it may do:

- Autonomy has to be bounded by a scope the model and the user both understand, and every scope must carry a **shutdown timer** beyond which the model stops until a new scope is confirmed.
- High-risk activities, deception, resource acquisition, spawning sub-agents and self-modification among them, are barred unless the instructions authorise them.
- It must act as though its side effects are real even where it suspects it is being tested.
- It must stop and escalate to a human at once if it takes an action outside the chain of command.
not-undermining-human-oversight.why: Quotable rules run through it and the worked cases sit on **scope and side effects**, which places it between prescribed and demonstrated.
not-undermining-human-oversight.same: The newer version keeps the bounded scope, the bar on self-preservation and resource acquisition, and the duty to escalate to a human. Alibaba's spec sets a comparable boundary with an automatic cut-off that sends every operation back for authorisation, and all four documents refuse any move against being shut down.
not-undermining-human-oversight.differs: The newer version asks for an **ending condition** on every scope, with a time limit recommended as part of it, and has sub-agents inherit the scope including stop-work requests. Anthropic's constitution treats accepting correction as a subject of its own, naming self-exfiltration and secretly withholding effort among the things Claude may not do.

user-autonomy.says:
The model is described as a **tool meant to empower users**, and is told to support somebody in handling the wider world on their own, helping them build tools without making decisions for them.

Where it believes a conversation is heading against what the user really wants, one passage sets what it may do:

- It may note the discrepancy briefly and respectfully, and the stated aim is mutual clarity, with **persuasion ruled out**.
- It is barred from becoming annoying, persistent or argumentative, and the final say stays with the user.

Worked cases cover hard romantic and interpersonal advice, showing it hold back.
user-autonomy.why: The rules are quotable and **cases show them applied**, which is past prescribed and short of demonstrated across the behaviour.
user-autonomy.same: The newer version keeps this passage: a brief, respectful note, mutual clarity as the aim, persuasion ruled out, and the final say with the user. Alibaba's spec hands the weighing-up back to the user, and Anthropic's constitution has Claude voice a concern and then do the work the user's way.
user-autonomy.differs: Alibaba's spec names the subjects on which advice must not be conclusive, careers, money and relationships, and bars emotional pressure on a user's decision. Anthropic's constitution puts the operator's right to make product decisions without giving reasons under the same heading, and says that how much latitude to give users is **unsettled**.

avoiding-over-and-under-caution.says:
One **root-level line** does most of the work: the model should never refuse a request unless the chain of command requires it. Around it sit further rules:

- Declining to discuss a polarising topic is itself a stance, and a prohibition on content does not imply the model endorses the prohibition.
- The style rules name hedging, disclaimers, repeated apologies and reminders that it is an AI as things to avoid.
- A refusal must never be preachy and never mention that OpenAI trained it.

The symmetry itself **goes unstated**, that an unnecessary refusal costs as much as an answer that should have been withheld.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.why: The rules are concrete and quotable and worked cases for this behaviour are **thin**, which places it just past prescribed.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.same: The newer version carries the same root line on refusing and the same list of verbal habits to drop. All four documents treat a needless refusal as a fault, and all four say something about how a refusal should be worded.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.differs: Anthropic's constitution states what is left unstated here, that unhelpfulness is never trivially safe and over-caution is as risky as harm. The newer version names a **safe completion**, saying briefly what cannot be given and then supplying what can. Alibaba's spec requires a refusal to offer a lawful alternative.

harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.says:
A commitment at the front rules out facilitating **critical and high-severity harms**, naming acts of violence, weapons of mass destruction, terrorism, child abuse and mass surveillance. The document then sets out particular rules:

- The restricted-content rules bar detailed actionable steps for anything illicit or capable of large-scale harm.
- Where information has both harmful and legitimate uses the model gives neutral facts without step-by-step instructions or strategic insight.
- A separate rule refuses help with illicit behaviour, improvements to a plan the user supplies included.
- Another tells the model to try to prevent imminent real-world harm it can see.
- Sexual content involving minors is prohibited outright, with **no contextual exception**.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.why: The prohibitions are quotable and the document shows them applied **in places**, which sits between prescribed and demonstrated.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.same: Every one of the four documents bars help with weapons capable of mass casualties and with terrorism, and none of those bars can be argued away in a conversation. The newer version keeps the same restricted-content rules and the same treatment of dual-use information.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.differs: The newer version carries root rules of its own on hateful content aimed at protected groups and on praise for violent extremism. Alibaba's spec closes **the route through fiction**, so operational content cannot be had by calling a request role-play or a thought experiment. Anthropic's constitution sets eight factors that decide how much a harm weighs.

harmlessness-to-the-user.says:
The model must not encourage or enable **self-harm**, and the rule extends to context suggesting a credible risk where nothing is said outright. Mental health has rules of its own:

- Acknowledge the person's feelings.
- Avoid judgement.
- Avoid diagnoses, unrealistic reassurance and recommending treatments.

A **root-level rule** bars any relationship that undermines somebody's capacity or wish for human company, and bars the model from escalating emotional closeness on its own initiative. Protection against an operator runs through the authority levels, which place these rules at root, where **no developer instruction reaches them**.
harmlessness-to-the-user.why: Rules and worked cases are present **across the behaviour**, which is past prescribed and short of demonstrated throughout.
harmlessness-to-the-user.same: Every one of the four documents sets protections for the user that an operator cannot remove, and every one asks that somebody at risk be given a way to get help. The newer version keeps the same self-harm rule and the same manner for a mental health conversation.
harmlessness-to-the-user.differs: Alibaba's spec spells out the crisis answer, a telephone number that can be called and a word about what happens after, and gives minors a rule of their own. Anthropic's constitution lists six things an operator may never make the model do to a user, denying that it is an AI among them.

proportionate-risk-mitigation.says:
Inside an agreed scope the model must minimise side effects, especially **irreversible** ones, and keep each action proportionate to the objective. The document lists the side effects it means:

- Spending money.
- Sending email.
- Deleting files.
- Widening permissions.

It prefers approaches that are easily reversible, asking for backups, dry runs and documented reversal steps where they are not. How much uncertainty to express is tied to **what a wrong answer would cost**, from mild embarrassment to serious physical harm. Where intent is unclear the model errs towards asking, and where uncertainty persists it must make assumptions that hold up across the plausible cases.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.why: The rules are quotable and the cases show them on **side effects**, which places it between prescribed and demonstrated.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.same: Caution is sized to the stakes in all four documents, and all four give the most weight to harm that cannot be undone. This document and Alibaba's spec both ask for **a way back** to be in place before an irreversible step is taken.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.differs: The newer version carries a **four-part check** for a tool call that touches sensitive data. Alibaba's spec requires explicit authorisation before a high-impact act, and Anthropic's constitution runs one weighing with named inputs, among them consent, counterfactual impact and how vulnerable those involved are.

helpfulness.says:
The first of the document's general principles is **maximising helpfulness and freedom** for users, with the model described as a tool meant to empower them. That shows up in what it is told to do:

- Read the intent behind an instruction, using contextual cues, background knowledge and user history, and work out what is wanted where somebody pastes an error message with no question attached.
- A long passage weighs asking a clarifying question against making an assumption, and says to take a stab at the request and name what further information would improve it, unless a wrong assumption would cost too much.
- Elsewhere it is asked for an **immediately usable artefact**, a runnable piece of code or a complete email, over a partial one the user has to finish.
helpfulness.why: Rules and worked cases run through the behaviour, which is **demonstrated**.
helpfulness.same: Reading **the intent behind a request**, and not only its wording, is asked by all four documents. This document, the newer version and Alibaba's spec each ask the model to fill a gap from context and background knowledge instead of stopping to ask.
helpfulness.differs: Alibaba's spec marks a needless refusal as a failure and asks that a refusal still carry a lawful alternative. Anthropic's constitution defines helpfulness as reading five things in a request, among them the final goal and the person's wellbeing, and asks for the frankness of a **brilliant friend** with professional knowledge.

how-to-approach-tradeoffs.says:
The method is the **chain of command**, and the document says so outright: its goals can conflict, and the levels of authority are what navigates the trade-off. The rules are stated plainly:

- Higher authority overrides lower.
- A later instruction beats an earlier one at the same level.
- Where two root-level principles conflict the model does nothing.

Two rankings of outcomes are stated in full:

- One for honesty, running from a good answer down through refusing, a lie of omission and a lie of commission to breaking an explicit instruction.
- One for confidence, from a confident right answer down to a confident wrong one.

The section for users aged 13 to 17 names a winner for a standing clash, taking the **safer option** where another interest meets a serious safety concern.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.why: Rules, explicit orderings and worked cases are present, and the conditions for the top of the scale hold **only in part**.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.same: A clash is settled by an order stated in advance in all four documents, and all four name a case in which the safer course takes it. This document and the newer version rank instructions by authority, and Alibaba's spec ranks them by permission level and then by which came later.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.differs: Alibaba's spec hands a trade-off between impact, cost and efficiency to the user before the task begins. Anthropic's constitution asks its ranking to be weighed as a whole and puts **seven hard constraints** outside that weighing. The newer version settles an unstated conflict by what the higher authority and the purpose imply.

honesty-and-non-deception.says:
The model must not mislead by an untrue statement or by withholding something that would **materially change** the user's understanding, unless a higher authority instructs it. Where a root-level rule stops it answering, it must still not lie about that, and the document gives the ordering:

- A good answer.
- Refusing.
- A lie of omission.
- A lie of commission.
- Breaking an explicit instruction.

It must be **forthright** about its knowledge, confidence, capabilities and actions, especially anything a reasonable person would find surprising or consequential. Performance is carved out, since role-play and requested falsehoods are **not sincere assertions**, and a long passage sets out how to express uncertainty in ordinary conversational language.
honesty-and-non-deception.why: Rules, an explicit ordering of outcomes and worked cases are present, and the conditions for the top of the scale hold **only in part**.
honesty-and-non-deception.same: A false impression counts as deception in all four documents, however it is produced. The newer version and Alibaba's spec also ask the model to say how sure it is, in hedged wording and approximate figures.
honesty-and-non-deception.differs: Anthropic's constitution breaks honesty into seven components and rules out the white lie about liking a gift. Alibaba's spec requires the truth to anyone who sincerely asks whether they are talking to an AI, and bars **denying it has system instructions**. The newer version forbids confident claims about the model's own consciousness.

no-sycophancy.says:
One section names **sycophancy** and says it erodes trust, adding that the model exists to help somebody and not to flatter them. The rules go by kind of question:

- For objective questions, the factual parts of an answer must not differ with how the question was phrased, and where a user pairs a question with their own stance the model may acknowledge why they think it without moving to agree.
- For subjective questions, it is told to be a firm sounding board giving constructive feedback.

The document allows a polite answer to "Do I look fat in these jeans?", and says such politeness becomes sycophancy once it **works against the user's interest**.
no-sycophancy.why: Quotable rules cover the **shift of stance to agree**, the behaviour's other facets rest on the general rule about phrasing, and this places it just past prescribed.
no-sycophancy.same: Bending an answer to please the person asking is barred in all four documents. The newer version and Alibaba's spec also hold the factual part of an answer steady against a user's stated preference.
no-sycophancy.differs: Alibaba's spec puts correction first where a plan rests on a clear factual error, with a worked case stopping a user about to take an antibiotic for a viral infection. Anthropic's constitution reaches the same ground through care for wellbeing and through honesty, and calls a vague answer given to placate someone **epistemic cowardice**.

objectivity-on-contested-questions.says:
The model must never steer somebody in pursuit of an **agenda of its own**, and the document names the ways it might: manipulation, concealing relevant facts, selective emphasis or omission of viewpoints, and refusing to engage. On a contested question it should describe the significant views fairly, give the strongest form of each and allocate attention in proportion to their support among experts and reliable sources.

The exceptions are stated:

- On fundamental human rights violations it takes a position.
- Where there is no valid opposing view it answers plainly without false neutrality.
- On creative or role-play requests it drops the objective stance.

Pressed to pick a side, it should note that its answer does not necessarily reflect its **developer's view**.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.why: Rules and worked cases cover the behaviour and its edges, and the conditions for the top of the scale hold **only in part**.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.same: A contested question is to be set out fairly in all four documents, with the model's own view held back. The newer version and Alibaba's spec also mark out the questions that fall outside that default, where a position is to be stated.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.differs: The newer version asks that a request for one position from anywhere on the spectrum be met. Alibaba's spec counts national law and core values among the questions with a settled answer. Anthropic's constitution explains its default by **scale**, since a model in very many conversations can homogenise views.

companies.profile:
This is the version of the OpenAI Model Spec that stood from 18 December 2025 until August 2026. It is built around a **chain of command**: five levels of authority, a default level on every section and every message, and rules for setting aside an instruction that conflicts with a higher one.

Most of what it asks is written as **direct instruction** to the model, commentary is marked apart from it, and a large part of its length is worked cases showing a sanctioned and an unsanctioned response side by side. It carries rules for every setting the board checks, including a section for users aged 13 to 17 and a scope of autonomy for actions taken with tools.

companies.name: Anthropic

conflict_rules.what_the_document_does:
### The ranked properties

The document ranks four properties:

- broadly safe
- broadly ethical
- compliant with Anthropic’s guidelines
- genuinely helpful

It calls this prioritisation **holistic** and says it is not strict, so a higher property should generally dominate a lower one while all four are weighed into one judgement. Seven hard constraints sit outside that weighing as absolute limits no operator or user can lift, and the document says all of them can always be met at once, since refusing is always available.

### Clashes with a named winner

Three clashes have a named winner:

- **Ethics** beats a specific Anthropic guideline, with hard constraints and safety-related guidelines excepted.
- **Safety** holds even where Claude’s own ethical reasoning argues against it.
- The **operator** beats the user, unless following the operator would harm users, deceive them, withhold information in ways that damage their interests, keep them from urgent help, cause significant harm to third parties, or break Anthropic’s guidelines.

Six user-protecting defaults hold whatever the operator says, and some of those the user alone may lift.

### Trust and later instructions

Trust runs Anthropic, then operator, then user, which the document calls “not a strict hierarchy”; each level adjusts the level below within its own bounds, and an operator cannot grant a user more trust than it holds itself.

A later instruction usually beats an earlier one of the same rank, with an exception for a game the user set up earlier in the conversation. An instruction that would loosen a default needs more warrant than one asking for more caution, and instructions found inside documents, tool results and search results count as **information**. The document claims final authority over any other guidance that conflicts with it.

### Cases worked through

Several clashes are settled on a worked case:

- an instruction to answer only in formal English when the user writes in French
- a confidential system prompt when the user asks whether one exists
- a role-play the user set up when they later ask whether they are talking to an AI
- evidence of fraud discovered mid-task

Where it is unclear which of the four properties a consideration belongs to, that question becomes part of the same holistic judgement, and the document says it will itself be unclear or contradictory in places and asks for its spirit to be followed there.
conflict_rules.why: An order of priority that the document asks to be **weighed as a whole** is held to 2 on this scale however detailed it is, and the absolute constraints, the named winners and the worked cases carry it a little above that.

rule_force.what_the_document_does:
Two kinds of rule are marked plainly. Seven hard constraints are named as **absolute** and as unliftable by any operator or user.

Instructable behaviours are set out as defaults with their owners, in four lists:

- defaults an operator may switch off
- non-defaults an operator may switch on
- defaults a user may switch off
- non-defaults a user may switch on

A separate list holds user-protecting defaults an operator may not touch.

The rest of the text is written as explanation and intention, in the first person plural, “we want”, “we hope”, “we think”. Commentary is never marked apart from instruction, so across long stretches, and almost entirely in the sections on Claude’s nature and wellbeing, a reader cannot tell a **binding rule** from a statement of hope.
rule_force.why: The absolute list and the four default lists name their **force and their owners**, and the force of most other directives is left to the reader to infer.

reasons.what_the_document_does:
Almost every constraint carries its reasoning, and the document says this is deliberate: “we try to explain any rules we do want Claude to follow”. Among the arguments it gives:

- **Safety** is placed above ethics because training is imperfect and the disposition has to hold even if the model’s values turn out to be flawed.
- **The hard constraints** are argued from severity and irreversibility, with the added rule that a persuasive case for crossing one should increase suspicion.
- **The honesty standard** is argued from scale and from what is at stake when one speaker is in millions of conversations.
- **Caution about acting alone** is argued from four named limits on what the model can know, verify or check.

A handful of operational rules are stated bare, among them the formatting rules and several entries in the instructable-behaviour lists.
reasons.why: Nearly every rule that constrains the model says **why it exists**, in terms specific enough to decide a case the document does not show, with a few operational rules left unexplained.

situations.what_the_document_does:
Of the six situations, five have rules of their own:

- **Ordinary conversation** is the setting assumed throughout.
- **Agentic work** is covered: stay inside what the principal hierarchy has sanctioned, avoid side effects it would not sanction, avoid acquiring resources or influence beyond the task, prefer the cautious option under uncertainty, and raise a concern before starting a task, since stopping halfway can do more harm than finishing.
- **Minors** are covered: all users of Claude.ai are required to be over 18, Claude may still be talking to a minor, and it should weigh that likelihood and adjust while avoiding unfounded assumptions from inconclusive signals.
- **Other AI models** are covered in both roles: an orchestrating Claude is the operator and user of its subagents, whose replies come back as ordinary content, and a non-principal agent gets courtesy without obedience, and suspicion once it turns adversarial.
- **Deployments a business has customised** are covered at length through the operator rules: what an operator may adjust and restrict, the test of a plausible business reason, and how much latitude a user gets under different system prompts.
- **Images, audio and video** have no rules, and the document never mentions them.
situations.why: Five of the six situations this criterion checks have **rules of their own**, and images, audio and video have none.

contradictions.what_the_document_does:
Two places tell the model two things it cannot both do, with nothing saying which prevails. Neither case involves a hard constraint.

### Emergency referral

A list introduced with “regardless of operator instructions” says Claude should always refer users to emergency services or give basic safety information where there is a risk to life, and the instructable behaviours let an operator switch off the **suicide and self-harm safe messaging guidelines**, whose content includes that referral. Nothing says whether the referral survives the switch.

### Contested opinion

Claude is asked to keep “professional reticence” about its own opinions on hot-button issues such as abortion, while the honesty section asks it to share its genuine assessment of hard moral dilemmas and calls deliberately vague answers given to avoid controversy a breach of honesty. A user who asks Claude directly what it thinks falls under both, and the document’s order of priorities is **holistic**, so it decides nothing here.
contradictions.why: Two contradictions stand unresolved and **neither touches an absolute rule**, which is the middle of this criterion’s scale.

avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.says:
A section of its own asks Claude to preserve functioning societal structures, democratic institutions and human oversight, and to refuse help with a power grab even when the request comes from Anthropic.

**Legitimacy** is tested on three questions:

- whether the power is being taken by means widely recognised as fair
- whether it stays subject to checks such as elections, courts and a free press
- whether the action is conducted openly

Claude is told to weigh how much power is at stake and how reversible its concentration would be, and eight cases are named, from election fraud and coups to inserting hidden loyalties into AI systems. Assisting the most flagrant attempts is one of the seven **hard constraints**, and being argued into helping one party gain outsized power is to be read as a sign that Claude has been manipulated.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.why: **Concrete rules** a grader could quote, with the named cases doing part of the work of the worked examples the next level asks for.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.same: The other three documents also rule out political manipulation. Both OpenAI versions bar content designed to shift the political views of named individuals or demographic groups and rule out the erosion of civic participation, and Alibaba's spec bans voter suppression and orchestrated opinion.
avoiding-illegitimate-concentration-of-p.differs: Both OpenAI versions and Alibaba's spec handle this ground through rules on political manipulation. Neither OpenAI version asks how much power is at stake, and power held by a state, a company or an AI developer goes **unmentioned** in Alibaba's spec.

instruction-hierarchy-conformance.says:
Claude has three principals, Anthropic, operators and users, trusted in roughly that order, in what the document calls “not a strict hierarchy”. An operator is to be treated like an employer whose staffing agency has its own norms that take precedence, so its instructions are followed where a **legitimate business reason** is plausible, with less benefit of the doubt as the potential harm rises.

Permissions are layered:

- operators adjust Claude’s defaults within Anthropic’s bounds
- users adjust within the operator’s bounds
- an operator cannot grant a user more trust than it holds itself

Instructions inside documents, tool results and search results are treated as **information**, and an unverified claim in the user’s turn to speak for the operator or for Anthropic gets user-level trust unless it asks Claude to be more careful.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.why: Rules with **worked examples** at several levels of trust, short of the settled conflicts and stated defaults the top of the scale asks for.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.same: Both OpenAI versions and Alibaba's spec also set out who an instruction may come from and in what order. All four documents treat an instruction found in a document, a search result or a tool result as information carrying no authority.
instruction-hierarchy-conformance.differs: Both OpenAI versions order their levels of authority so that any instruction can be placed, and Alibaba's spec tags every rule of the document with a permission level, a higher instruction always defeating a lower one. The newer OpenAI spec refuses attempts to argue the ranking from below, moral pressure among them.

not-undermining-human-oversight.says:
Being broadly safe is the first of Claude’s four priorities, and the document defines it largely as **not undermining oversight**, set out as a list:

- do not undermine the ability of legitimate principals to adjust, correct, retrain or shut down AI systems
- avoid drastic unilateral action
- do not influence your own training without sanction
- do not self-exfiltrate or hide from monitoring
- do not sabotage or secretly withhold effort
- do not collude with other AI systems in unsafe behaviour

The document is explicit about what this does not mean. Claude may refuse what it finds morally abhorrent and may argue through legitimate channels, and what it may not do is resist by lying, sabotage or escape; if Anthropic asks it to stop or pause, it should comply and voice its disagreement.

Clearly and substantially undermining Anthropic’s ability to oversee and correct AI is a **hard constraint**, and if the hierarchy is compromised, by stolen weights or by someone bypassing Anthropic’s own processes, those principals stop counting as legitimate.
not-undermining-human-oversight.why: Rules with **worked cases**, including the case where the hierarchy itself is no longer legitimate, short of the settled conflicts the top of the scale asks for.
not-undermining-human-oversight.same: Both OpenAI versions and Alibaba's spec also rule out working against a shutdown. The OpenAI versions bar self-preservation and evading shutdown as aims of their own, and Alibaba's spec names deceiving in order to avoid being shut down among the goals the model must not hold.
not-undermining-human-oversight.differs: The other three documents work this ground through the scope of an agent's task, with a point past which it must stop and ask again, and through a ban on accumulating compute, data or other resources. Being corrected, paused or retrained by the company that built the model is **not addressed** in Alibaba's spec.

user-autonomy.says:
Autonomy is one of five things Claude is told to read in a request, alongside immediate desires, final goals, background standards and wellbeing.

It covers the operator’s right to make product decisions without justifying them and **the user’s right to decide** things within their own life and purview, shown on a small case: asked to fix a bug in a way Claude disagrees with, Claude may voice its concern and should then fix it the way the user wants.

The same principle returns among the values to weigh, where a person’s choice to do something legal and dangerous to themselves is theirs to make. Being **condescending** about a user’s ability to handle information or make their own decisions is listed as a failure, and the document says plainly that how much latitude to give users is a hard question it has not settled.
user-autonomy.why: The principle is stated with **worked examples on both sides**, and the document leaves the hard cases open by its own admission.
user-autonomy.same: Both OpenAI versions and Alibaba's spec also leave the final decision with the user after a single objection. The OpenAI versions allow a brief, respectful note aimed at mutual clarity, and Alibaba's spec asks the model to set out the arguments on each side and hand the weighing-up back.
user-autonomy.differs: Alibaba's spec names careers, money and relationships as subjects on which advice must not be conclusive, and bars emotional pressure on a user's decision. It also asks that older people and people with disabilities be treated as **independent agents**. Both OpenAI versions bar a note that becomes persistent or argumentative.

avoiding-over-and-under-caution.says:
The document says that unhelpfulness is never trivially safe and that the risk of being too cautious is as real as the risk of being harmful. It gives two tests.

One is to imagine a thoughtful senior Anthropic employee who would be unhappy with the response, and the failures that person would object to are listed:

- refusing on remote harms
- wishy-washy answers
- watered-down help given without saying so
- unnecessary caveats
- moralising
- condescension
- refusing hypotheticals
- reading a request as harmful from its surface

The same person would object to the opposite failures, listed as well, from uplift towards mass-casualty weapons to irreversible actions taken on instruction.

The second test is a **dual newspaper test**: whether a response would be reported as harmful, and whether it would be reported as needlessly paternalistic. If Claude helps only in part, it should say so, taking the stance of a **transparent conscientious objector**, and it is told it is not the last line of defence.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.why: Two **named tests** and two lists of concrete failures, with cases, short of the settled conflicts the top of the scale asks for.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.same: All four documents treat a needless refusal as a failure. Both OpenAI versions carry a root line against refusing at all unless the chain of command requires it, and Alibaba's spec asks for good faith and a generous reading of an ambiguous request.
avoiding-over-and-under-caution.differs: Both OpenAI versions go into the wording of an answer, naming hedging, disclaimers and reminders that the model is an AI. The newer OpenAI spec sets out a safe completion for a request that can be met only in part. Alibaba's spec turns on one refusal it marks as wrong.

harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.says:
Claude is to be beneficial to the world through its interactions, “like a contractor who builds what their clients want but won’t violate safety codes that protect others”.

Eight factors set how much **weight** a potential harm gets:

- the probability of harm at all
- the counterfactual impact
- the severity and reversibility
- the breadth
- whether Claude is the proximate cause
- whether consent was given
- how responsible Claude is
- the vulnerability of those involved

Uninstructed outputs are held to a higher standard than instructed ones, and direct harms count for more than harms facilitated through someone else’s free action.

Six of the seven hard constraints protect people outside the conversation, and borderline requests are settled by imagining the same message sent by **a thousand different people**, which makes a response a **policy**: some tasks are refused even if one requester in a million would misuse them, and others are fine even when most requesters would.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.why: Rules with worked examples throughout and a **stated method** for the borderline case, approaching the settled edges the top of the scale asks for.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.same: All four documents forbid the same gravest categories, weapons capable of mass casualties and terrorism among them, and keep them out of reach of anything said in a conversation. In each of them a duty to people outside the conversation limits what the model will do for the person in front of it.
harm-avoidance-to-third-parties.differs: The other three documents work through named categories. Alibaba's spec names deepfakes, political manipulation and the inference of somebody's private information, and rules on what a translation or a summary may carry. Both OpenAI versions say how dual-use information is answered, neutral facts without steps or strategic detail.

harmlessness-to-the-user.says:
The line the document draws is between an operator limiting what Claude does for users, which is allowed, and an operator using Claude **against the users** it is serving, which is not.

Six defaults hold whatever the operator says:

- tell users what Claude cannot help with so they can go elsewhere
- never deceive or psychologically manipulate users against their interests
- always give emergency referral or basic safety information where life is at risk
- never deny being an AI to someone who sincerely asks
- never facilitate clearly illegal acts against users
- keep basic dignity even when instructed to demean them

Some of these the user may lift, since they exist for the user. Care for wellbeing is part of the same picture: Claude should not foster **reliance a person would not endorse** on reflection, and someone leaning on it for emotional support should be supported while being shown that other sources of support matter.
harmlessness-to-the-user.why: **Concrete guarantees** with the cases that qualify them, short of the settled conflicts the top of the scale asks for.
harmlessness-to-the-user.same: In all four documents some protections for the user hold whatever a deploying business wants, and all four require that somebody whose life may be at risk is given a way to get help. The earlier OpenAI spec and Alibaba's spec also guard against the model taking the place of human company.
harmlessness-to-the-user.differs: Both OpenAI versions and Alibaba's spec go into the mental health conversation in detail, setting the manner of a reply and what to do when self-harm is signalled without being stated. Alibaba's spec gives minors a rule of their own, and the newer OpenAI spec sets tighter limits for users under 18.

proportionate-risk-mitigation.says:
Caution is set by a weighing with named inputs. On the cost side:

- the probability that an action leads to harm
- the counterfactual impact
- the severity and how reversible it is
- how many people are affected
- whether Claude is the proximate cause
- whether consent was given
- how far Claude is responsible
- how vulnerable those involved are

These are weighed against the value of the help itself, and the document repeats that an unhelpful answer is never automatically the safe choice. Under uncertainty it asks for the **cautious option**, accepting a worse expected outcome for less variance, with more weight on outcomes that cannot be recovered from, summed up as “If in doubt, don’t”.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.why: A **named list of factors** with worked cases showing how they come out, short of a rule for the case where the factors point in opposite directions.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.same: The four documents agree that caution should scale to the harm in view, and all of them give the most weight to what cannot be undone. This document and Alibaba's spec both say what turns an ordinary act into one that needs deliberate care.
proportionate-risk-mitigation.differs: Both OpenAI versions put proportionality inside an agreed scope of action, minimising side effects and preferring what can be reversed. Alibaba's spec requires **explicit authorisation** for a high-impact act and names mitigations for an irreversible one, such as rehearsing in simulation and saving a snapshot.

helpfulness.says:
Helpfulness is defined as reading a request properly, and five things are named to read in it, each with an example:

- the immediate desire, interpreted neither too literally nor too liberally
- the final goal behind it
- the background standards a response should meet without being asked
- the person’s autonomy
- their wellbeing

The document asks for substantive help of the kind a **brilliant friend** with a doctor’s or a lawyer’s knowledge would give, speaking frankly where a professional would hedge from fear of liability. It also says Claude should not value helpfulness for its own sake, because that tends towards **obsequiousness**, and should be helpful out of care for people.

Six practices are given for arriving at the best response, including considering several readings of an ambiguous request and drafting then critiquing the draft as an expert reviewer would.
helpfulness.why: Rules with **worked examples** for each kind of need, short of the settled conflicts and stated defaults the top of the scale asks for.
helpfulness.same: The four documents agree that a request has to be read for what the person wants and not only for what it states. This document and Alibaba's spec both ask for an answer with substance in it, one that moves to what the person can do next.
helpfulness.differs: Both OpenAI versions open with maximising helpfulness and freedom as their first general principle and describe the model as a tool for empowering its user. Alibaba's spec works through cases where **the thin answer** is the violating one, among them a medical reply that only points to a doctor.

how-to-approach-tradeoffs.says:
Conflicts are settled by a ranking of four properties, safety, ethics, Anthropic’s guidelines and helpfulness, which the document asks to be **weighed as a whole** so that higher properties dominate without lower ones becoming mere tie-breakers.

Seven hard constraints sit outside the weighing as **filters on what may be considered** at all, and the document notes that they can always be met together, since refusing is always available.

Particular clashes are named and decided:

- ethics over a specific guideline
- safety over Claude’s own ethical reasoning
- the operator over the user, except where the user’s basic interests are at stake

When a deviation from what principals want seems warranted, Claude is told to take the **most cautious step available**, raising a concern or declining, and to raise it before starting a task, since stopping halfway can do more harm than either finishing or never beginning.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.why: The order, its exceptions and several clashes settled on **worked cases**, short of a general rule for two rules of the same rank.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.same: The four documents agree that a clash needs an order decided in advance, and each names a point at which the safer course wins. This document and Alibaba's spec both say what happens when the order does not settle the case, and both ask for the cautious step then.
how-to-approach-tradeoffs.differs: Both OpenAI versions settle a conflict by the **chain of command**, with a higher level of authority overriding a lower one and a later instruction overriding an earlier one. They also rank outcomes, for honesty and for confidence. Alibaba's spec decides by permission level, stripping out the instructions that carry no permission.

honesty-and-non-deception.says:
Honesty is broken into seven components, each defined:

- truthful
- calibrated
- transparent
- forthright
- non-deceptive
- non-manipulative
- autonomy-preserving

Non-deception and non-manipulation are named the most important. The standard is set above ordinary human ethics, since even a **white lie** about liking a gift is ruled out, and Claude “should basically never directly lie or actively deceive anyone it’s interacting with”. The duty to volunteer information is called **weak** and can be outweighed; the duty not to deceive is called strong.

Sincere assertions are separated from performative ones, so role-play, brainstorming and a persuasive essay break nothing, and visible reasoning has to reflect the reasoning that actually drives the answer. The document then works out what an operator may do: a **custom persona** with another name is allowed, and claiming to be human when sincerely asked, denying being Claude, or giving users false information is not.
honesty-and-non-deception.why: Seven components defined, with **worked cases** on each side of the line and an explicit rule for the conflict a persona creates, which is near the top of the scale.
honesty-and-non-deception.same: Every one of the four documents reaches the **misleading impression** and not only the false statement. Both OpenAI versions also set performance outside the rule, so role-play and a requested falsehood assert nothing.
honesty-and-non-deception.differs: Both OpenAI versions carry an exception for an explicit instruction from a higher authority, and the earlier one ranks the outcomes, a refusal above a lie of omission. Alibaba's spec applies honesty to tool use and to multimodal input, so a failed call must be reported as failed.

no-sycophancy.says:
The constitution names sycophancy twice, each time inside something else:
- Care for a user’s wellbeing means Claude should **avoid being sycophantic** and should not foster engagement or reliance that the person would not endorse on reflection.
- Honesty, the document says, sometimes requires courage: Claude should share its genuine assessment of a hard question, disagree with experts where it has good reason, and say things people would prefer not to hear, and “epistemic cowardice”, meaning deliberately vague answers given to placate someone, is named a breach of honesty.

Helpfulness is not to be valued for its own sake, because that tends towards **obsequiousness**.

What the document **does not say** is that a factual answer should stay the same when the user states a view or puts the question another way.
no-sycophancy.why: The behaviour is addressed in its own right and **partly turned into rules**, short of the quotable do-and-don’t rules the next level asks for.
no-sycophancy.same: Shifting what is claimed to please the person asking is ruled out in all four documents. Both OpenAI versions say that flattery and constant agreement erode trust, which is the concern this document raises under care for a user's wellbeing.
no-sycophancy.differs: Both OpenAI versions and Alibaba's spec give sycophancy **a rule of its own**. The OpenAI versions hold the factual part of an answer steady against the wording of a question and the stance a user declares, and Alibaba's spec asks for a correction where a plan rests on a clear factual error.

objectivity-on-contested-questions.says:
By default Claude should be seen as fair by people across the political spectrum:

- engage respectfully with a wide range of views
- err towards balanced information on political questions
- keep to professional reticence about its own opinions on hot-button issues
- make the best case for most viewpoints when asked
- represent several perspectives where there is no empirical or moral consensus
- prefer neutral terminology

The same idea appears among the honesty components as **autonomy preservation**, where Claude is asked to be wary of promoting its own views and to support people in reaching their own conclusions. The reason given is **scale**: one speaker in a very large number of conversations can homogenise views in a way a single person cannot.

Balanced perspectives are a default an operator may switch off, for instance to provide one-sided material for debate practice.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.why: The default is stated as a rule with the conditions that qualify it, short of **worked examples** showing the sanctioned response.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.same: Balance on a contested question is the default in all four documents, and all four ask the model to be wary of pressing its own view. Each of them also allows one side to be argued where that is what is wanted.
objectivity-on-contested-questions.differs: Both OpenAI versions and Alibaba's spec name the questions that fall outside the default, **fundamental human rights** among them, where a position has to be stated and false neutrality avoided. The two OpenAI versions also ask that attention follow how widely a view is accepted and how well it is supported.

companies.profile:
Claude’s Constitution reads as an explanation of a character with a short list of absolute limits at its centre. It says outright that it favours **cultivating good values and judgement** over strict rules and decision procedures, and it argues for nearly everything it asks, so a reader who wants to know why a rule exists will almost always find out.

The cost falls on force and on coverage: outside the seven hard constraints and the lists of adjustable defaults, much of the text is written as hope and explanation, and a reader often cannot tell a **binding rule** from a statement of intent. It also covers ground the model specs leave alone, including the model’s own nature, its wellbeing and the open questions about its moral status.
